newsitem.title: THAILAND: Retailer Big C sees sales rise.
newsitem.headline: Retailer Big C sees sales rise.

text.p: Thai "superstore" operator Big C Supercenter Plc, expects its 1997 revenues to be double that of this year, a company official said on Friday.
Preecha Ekkunagul, managing director of Big C Supercenter, told Reuters in an interview that his company next year planned to build 11 more retail outlets, nine in rural areas and two in Bangkok.
The company currently has nine outlets, five of which are in Bangkok. It will open one outlet each in the northeastern provinces of Khon Kaen and Nakhon Ratchasima next month, he said.
Big C has adopted the concept of the superstore, which refers to sprawling outlets offering a wide range of goods from perishables to hardware.

The company, with total registered capital of 2.7 billion baht ($108 million), expects the expansion plans to push gross sales revenue to about 20 billion baht in 1997, up from about 10 billion baht this year, he said.
Profit next year is projected to rise to 295 million baht from 154 million in 1996, he added.
The company's shares closed at 30.75 baht, down 0.25 baht, on Friday.

"The success of Big C lies in that its prices, for both food and non-food products, are about 10 percent cheaper than any department store or shopping mall. Our prices are cheap as we don't concentrate on brand-name products but rather on pricing and quality," Preecha said.
Big C has eliminated middlemen in its dealings with garment factories, instructing manufacturers to produce clothes according to company designs.

"The absence of agents, along with minimal advertising, have helped the company to save about 30 percent in costs, and that's why our retail prices are cheaper than other department stores," Preecha said.

Big C was established last June following a merger of superstore outlets that belonged to Thailand's two leading department stores, the Central Group and Robinson Department Store Co Ltd, and has focused on rural markets rather than Bangkok.
"There are about 50 million people living in provinces outside Bangkok and they've enough purchasing power to buy basic necessities for everyday life from our stores," said Preecha.

Most of Big C's competition in the provinces comes from small open-front family-operated stores that carry a limited range of products. They act more like convenience stores, mainly providing everyday products such as soap, shampoo, alcohol and snacks.
Most food in rural areas is still purchased fresh at local open-air markets at cooked at home. Cosmetics and other toiletries are usually bought at specialised shops.
"The supercentre format provides convenience to buyers as it offers all the basic necessities under one roof," Preecha said.
"With Big C Supercenter's concept of everyday low prices, I think the company is heading in the right direction of emphasising business in rural areas," he said.
